Production tooling that verifies 'as-built matches as-designed' overwhelmingly relies on machine-checkable companion artifacts rather than NLP-parsed prose.
claims.notes: Unanimous finding across nine surveyed production systems.

claims.text: All nine production systems surveyed (Nygard ADR, MADR, Archgate, ADR Kit (kschlt), DECIDER, adr-kit (rvdbreemen), ArchUnit, Pact, OpenAPI/Schemathesis/Dredd, Spectral, Terraform Sentinel/OPA) use machine-checkable companion artifacts; none use NLP-parsing of prose for verification.

The canonical Nygard ADR template (2011) is a five-section Markdown document (Title, Status, Context, Decision, Consequences) with no machine-readable companion artifact and no mechanism for automated verification that code conforms to the decision.
The Nygard ADR format is optimized for human comprehension and historical preservation, not for build-time enforcement; supersession is handled by marking old ADRs 'superseded' and preserving them.
Archgate pairs each Markdown ADR with a companion `.rules.ts` file that exports automated checks.
claims.notes: Finding 2; verbatim quote from Archgate CLI README (2026-02-23).

claims.text: kschlt/adr-kit generates ESLint and Ruff rules from an optional `policy` frontmatter block on each ADR.
DECIDER embeds ADR constraints, invariants, and scope as YAML frontmatter.
rvdbreemen's adr-kit reads a declarative JSON `## Enforcement` block from the ADR body.

Archgate, ADR Kit (kschlt), DECIDER, and adr-kit (rvdbreemen) all explicitly avoid NLP parsing of the ADR prose body for the enforcement layer — the rule lives in a parallel structured artifact while the prose retains the human-facing rationale.
claims.notes: Finding 2 — central convergence claim across four recent ADR toolkits.

claims.text: The four modern ADR toolkits (Archgate, ADR Kit, DECIDER, adr-kit) are recent (2025–2026) and not yet 'battle-tested at scale' in the way Pact or ArchUnit are.

claims.text: Structured MADR adds required YAML frontmatter validated against a JSON Schema; the GitHub Action `zircote/structured-madr@v1` fails the workflow when frontmatter is malformed.
Structured MADR's verification target is the ADR document's own structural integrity (valid metadata, intact relationships), not whether code obeys the decision.
ArchUnit encodes architecture rules directly as JUnit tests written in code, with the ADR referenced via the rule's `because(...)` clause rather than via a separate ADR document.
A 2025 PR (#1496) attempted to generate ADRs from ArchUnit rules; the maintainer rejected as out-of-scope, noting an ADR can reference a rule but rules cannot generate ADRs.
ArchUnit offers `FreezeRules` for legacy codebases to grandfather existing violations while preventing new ones.
ArchUnit's binding is to Java bytecode; it cannot enforce rules about non-Java assets (configs, infra).
Schema-based contracts (OpenAPI/JSON Schema) cannot express HTTP-level semantics such as verb, path, headers, and status code.
Schema-based contracts are abstract and ambiguous: `anyOf`/`oneOf` leave the mapping of inputs to status codes undefined.
Schema-based contracts cannot guarantee a system fully implements the spec; they verify only that behaviour is 'not incompatible with the spec'.
claims.notes: Finding 5; verbatim aphorism from Pact ecosystem.

claims.text: Schema-based contracts create a false sense of security when provider and consumer happen to validate non-overlapping schema subsets.
Code-based Pact contracts cost more to author but capture intent and conversation.
Schema-based contract tests sacrifice a level of guarantees in favour of a simpler developer experience.
The OpenAPI document itself (YAML/JSON) functions as spec-as-code — the machine-readable contract layer.
Schemathesis property-generates test cases from an OpenAPI spec and runs them against the implementation, catching schema violations, validation bypasses, and 500-error edge cases.
Spectral lints both the OpenAPI spec document and arbitrary YAML/JSON via custom rule files (`.spectral.yaml`), converting house-style decisions into rules rather than prose.
Spectral's rule format is JSONPath plus named functions; it cannot express arbitrary code-level constraints such as 'no DB call from controller'.

Terraform's mature policy-as-code stack (HashiCorp Sentinel and Open Policy Agent / Conftest) has converged on the pattern: policy is a separate executable file applied to a structured JSON representation of the build artifact.
The Terraform plan is exported via `terraform show -json`, then evaluated against Rego or Sentinel policies before `apply`.
HashiCorp Sentinel adds tiered enforcement levels (advisory, soft-mandatory, hard-mandatory) so policies can roll out gradually.

In Terraform policy-as-code, the decision rationale (why a policy exists) lives in policy comments or linked documentation, but the enforcement target is always the structured plan JSON, never the prose.
A 2026 vendor comparison estimates a 60% reduction in policy-violation incidents using policy-as-code (Sentinel/OPA) versus manual review.

claims.text: A 2026 arXiv paper (2602.07609) evaluated multiple LLMs (including a Large Reasoning Model with RAG) on detecting whether code complies with the Decision/Context/Consequence sections of an ADR.
LLMs struggle most on ADRs involving implicit architectural knowledge, cross-module dependencies, or domain-specific constraints.
In arXiv 2602.07609's evaluation of LLM-based ADR compliance checking, 44.57% of LLM errors were categorized as semantic or logical misinterpretation.
claims.notes: Finding 8 — load-bearing quantitative result; verbatim percentage.

claims.text: In arXiv 2602.07609, 28.26% of LLM errors were inability to infer implicit or missing context.

In arXiv 2602.07609, approximately 8.7% of LLM errors were categorized as overgeneralization.
arXiv 2602.07609 concludes that LLMs 'can meaningfully support architectural compliance checks, but cannot replace human reasoning or complementary analysis tools.'

claims.text: Multiple independent engineering blogs and pattern catalogues document the same anti-pattern: agent selection accuracy degrades sharply beyond roughly 10–20 tools per reasoning context.
claims.notes: Finding 8 — cross-platform anti-pattern consensus, 4-source corroboration (aipatternbook.com Tool Sprawl; agentpatterns.tech Too Many Tools 2026-03-16; tianpan.co Tool Explosion Problem 2026-04-13; kvg.dev Stop Drowning Your Agent in Tools 2026-01-10).

claims.text: Published thresholds indicate 5–10 tools is the practical sweet spot for agent tool selection.
The Berkeley Function Calling Leaderboard shows isolated tool-calling at ~96% accuracy dropping to ~13–15% in large-toolset multi-turn settings.
One widely-cited case study reports paring tools from 16 to 1 raised success from 80% to 100% with 40% lower tokens.
The mechanism for tool-proliferation degradation is consistently described as attention dilution / context rot from tool-description token competition.
Load-on-demand patterns (Anthropic progressive disclosure, OpenAI tool_search, LangGraph bigtool, MCP allowlist scoping) are the converging architectural defense against tool/skill proliferation.
claims.notes: Finding 8 caveat — converging architectural defense pattern.

claims.text: The closest cross-platform analog to a structured decision artifact is CrewAI's Crews-vs-Flows matrix, which is a runtime-architecture selector rather than a per-capability rationale.
claims.notes: Synthesis — structural-divergence claim about closest analog.

claims.text: The closest pre-design discipline cross-platform is Perplexity's 'write evals first' — a practice with a deliverable (the eval suite), not a document template.

The Why/How/Anti-patterns trifecta as a mandated, authored-at-design-time, per-capability artifact appears to be novel as a codification, even though every component of its content is well-trodden community substance.
claims.notes: Synthesis — novelty verdict for the trifecta.

claims.text: Across the surveyed sources, the same anti-patterns recur in 2024, 2025, and 2026 posts, suggesting that even teams who have read the principles continue to violate them in production.
claims.notes: Synthesis — prose-principles-produce-drift observation, motivates the trifecta mandate.

claims.text: The trifecta's contribution is forcing the rationale into a reviewable artifact, which creates an audit point so a reviewer can ask 'where's the rationale?' instead of inferring from code.
The trifecta concentrates the decision so that 'why-now' and 'what-could-go-wrong' sit next to each other instead of being scattered across docstrings, system prompts, and tribal memory.
The trifecta defends specifically against proliferation, which is the most universally-documented failure mode in the surveyed literature.

Every surveyed platform stops short of mandating a structured form for capability decisions, suggesting the cost of the mandate (overhead, ritualistic compliance, 'filling in the boxes' without thought) is non-trivial.
The trifecta will need anti-ritualism defenses (e.g., reviewers checking substance not presence) to avoid the ritualistic-compliance failure mode.
The trifecta's Anti-patterns section should default to a curated short list with rationale rather than an exhaustive catalogue, to avoid ritual.
Orphaned-capability decay is not named as a primary anti-pattern in the surveyed primary sources; the closest analog is Perplexity's drift-from-fast-changing-MCP-endpoint warning.
claims.notes: Open question — gap in literature about orphaned-capability decay.

claims.text: Surveyed platforms differ on what the unit of capability is (skill vs. plugin vs. function vs. specialist agent), so the trifecta's unit of mandate should be defined explicitly.
None of the surveyed sources prescribes review heuristics for capability-rationale documents, because none mandates such a document.
claims.notes: Open question — reviewer enforcement mechanics are green-field design space.
